claims.text: Formation and crystal-structure selection in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles are governed by the interplay between atomic size mismatch and electronic-structure compatibility.
Substituting constituent elements with elements having different atomic radii and electronic configurations will systematically vary atomic size mismatch and electronic-structure compatibility.
Atomic size mismatch introduces strain energy.

Atomic size mismatch and electronic-structure compatibility jointly determine whether rapid synthesis produces a thermodynamically stable single-phase solid solution or phase separation and elemental segregation.
Compositions with lower atomic size mismatch and higher electronic-structure compatibility are more likely to form a single-phase solid solution with a controlled crystal structure.
Compositions with higher atomic size mismatch or electronic-structure incompatibility are more likely to exhibit phase separation.
Compositions with higher atomic size mismatch or electronic-structure incompatibility are more likely to exhibit elemental segregation.
Compositions with higher atomic size mismatch or electronic-structure incompatibility are more likely to exhibit uncontrolled particle morphology.
The proposed relationship applies to noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing at least five elements under rapid heating and cooling.
The proposed relationship does not apply to systems with fewer elements or significantly different synthesis regimes.

contradictions.description: The initial state requires more than five elements, whereas the conditions and boundary allow at least five elements; a five-element composition is therefore simultaneously excluded and included.
